claims.claim: Becoming a good person is mainly a matter of your own effort and choices.

stances.original: Haec igitur prima sanctae ac spiritualis vitae fundamenta jaciantur, ut vires suas virgo agnoscat: quas demum bene exercere poterit, cum eas se habere didicerit. Optima enim animi incitamenta sunt, cum docetur aliquis posse quod cupiat.
stances.summary: God made human nature strong and able to choose the good. So the first thing to teach anyone who wants to live well is how much they can do. People fail because they believe goodness is beyond them.
stances.quote: So let these be laid as the first foundations of a holy and spiritual life: that the virgin should recognise her own strength. She will only be able to use it well once she has learned that she has it. For the best spur to the mind is being taught that you can do what you desire.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Latin (Migne, Patrologia Latina 30, as transcribed on Latin Wikisource)
stances.location: chapter 2 (PL 30:16-17, printed there among the spurious letters of Jerome as Letter 1)
stances.context: Written about 413 to Demetrias, a young Roman noblewoman who had just taken the veil. The letter opens by saying that whenever Pelagius teaches about the moral life he first shows "the power and quality of human nature" so that no one thinks virtue impossible. In chapter 16 he mocks people who tell God "It is hard, it is too steep, we cannot, we are only human, we are wrapped in frail flesh" and calls it "blind madness"; God, who knows our strength, "did not wish to command anything impossible" (Latin: "Durum est, arduum est, non possumus, homines sumus, fragili carne circumdamur. O caecam insaniam! O profanam temeritatem!"). To be fair to him, he does speak of grace: chapter 3 says Christians "are also helped by the aid of divine grace", and chapter 9 wants the virgin to witness to "the good of nature and of grace together". Augustine answered that by grace Pelagius meant nature, the law, teaching and forgiveness, not an inner help to the will. Pelagius himself claimed the letter in a letter to Pope Innocent, quoted by Augustine (On the Grace of Christ 1.40, NPNF). A blunter line of his survives only in Augustine's verbatim quotation of his lost book In Defence of Free Will: "that we really do a good thing, or speak a good word, or think a good thought, proceeds from our own selves" (On the Grace of Christ 1.5, NPNF 1st series vol. 5, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/15061.htm). Augustine also records that Pelagius, at Rome, "could not bear" Augustine's prayer "Give what You command, and command what You will" and nearly quarrelled with the bishop who quoted it (Gift of Perseverance 20.53). HETERODOX: Pelagius was condemned by the African councils (416, 418), by Pope Zosimus (418) and at the Council of Ephesus (431). No English translation before 1929 was found; the English in circulation (B. R. Rees, 1991) is copyrighted.

stances.person: Caelestius (Coelestius), associate of Pelagius (not in the results pool)
stances.summary: If God commands us to be without sin, then we are able to be without sin. A duty you cannot fulfil is not a duty.
stances.quote: We must again, he says, inquire whether a man ought to be without sin. Beyond doubt he ought. If he ought, he is able; if he is not able, then he ought not.
stances.translation: Peter Holmes and Robert Ernest Wallis, revised by Benjamin B. Warfield, NPNF 1st series vol. 5, 1887
stances.work: The Definitions ascribed to Caelestius, as quoted by Augustine in On Man's Perfection in Righteousness
stances.context: Augustine quotes these propositions word for word in order to answer each one. He says the paper was titled "The definitions, so it is said, of Caelestius" and that he is not sure they are Caelestius's own, though they match a work of his "undoubted" authorship. The words "he says" are Augustine's. Augustine's reply grants "if he ought, he is able" only for a lame man who is first healed: the will can do it once grace has cured it. HETERODOX: Caelestius was condemned at Carthage (411 and 418) and at Ephesus (431). Useful mainly as the plainest statement of the "you can, so you must" logic.

stances.summary: Virtue is not far away or outside us. It is our own soul kept as God made it, so all it needs from us is the will.
stances.quote: Wherefore virtue has need at our hands of willingness alone, since it is in us and is formed from us. For when the soul has its spiritual faculty in a natural state virtue is formed.
stances.translation: H. Ellershaw, NPNF 2nd series vol. 4, 1892
stances.work: Athanasius, Life of Antony (Antony's address to the monks)
stances.context: Part of the long speech Athanasius puts in Antony's mouth, written about 357-362, just after Antony's death in 356. Athanasius says he knew Antony well and "was his attendant for a long time". Just before, Antony says virtue "is not far from us, nor is it without ourselves, but it is within us, and is easy if only we are willing", and contrasts Greeks who cross the sea for learning with Christians who need not leave home for virtue. He is teaching that goodness is natural to the soul, not that grace is unneeded; the same Life, in Athanasius's own voice, calls Antony's victories "the Saviour's work in Antony" (chapter 7). The desert sayings also keep a warning in Antony's name: "I know monks who fell after many labours and lost their minds, because they had put their hope in their own work" (own rendering of the Greek alphabetical collection, Antony 37: "Οἶδα μοναχοὺς μετὰ πολλοὺς κό πους πεσόντας͵ καὶ εἰς ἔκστασιν φρενῶν ἐλθόντας͵ διὰ τὸ ἠλπικέναι ἐπὶ τὸ ἔργον αὐτῶν͵ καὶ παραλογι σαμένους τὴν ἐντολὴν τοῦ εἰπόντος· Ἐπερώτησον τὸν πατέρα σου͵ καὶ ἀναγγελεῖ σοι", http://www.ldysinger.com/@texts/0400_apophth/greek_alph/01_Introd_alpha-gamma.htm). Benedicta Ward's copyrighted English of that saying reads "Nine monks"; the Greek on the page reads "I know monks".

stances.summary: God did not make us like trees or animals that cannot choose. We are praised for good and blamed for evil only because we choose it ourselves.
stances.quote: for neither would he be worthy of reward or praise did he not of himself choose the good, but were created for this end; nor, if he were evil, would he be worthy of punishment, not being evil of himself, but being able to be nothing else than what he was made.
stances.translation: Marcus Dods and George Reith, ANF vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: Written about 155 to the emperor. Justin is answering the charge that Christian prophecy implies fate, and is arguing against pagan fatalism, not about grace; the chapter title in the translation is "Responsibility asserted". He says "it is by free choice they both walk uprightly and stumble". Elsewhere, in the Dialogue with Trypho 7, the old man who converts him says truth can be understood "only by the man to whom God and His Christ have imparted wisdom", which Justin records approvingly. So he held free choice firmly without a worked-out view of grace.

stances.summary: Knowledge comes to us from outside, from teaching. Virtue is entirely our own, because it lies in the will to do good.
stances.quote: Knowledge therefore consists in a benefit derived from another; for it depends upon hearing. Virtue is altogether our own; for it depends upon the will of doing that which is good.
stances.translation: William Fletcher, ANF vol. 7, 1886
stances.context: Written about 305-311 for educated pagans. Lactantius is correcting the Roman poet Lucilius, who defined virtue as knowledge. He goes on: knowing the way is useless "unless we also have the effort and strength for walking". The Institutes say little about grace; elsewhere in Book 6 Lactantius says the philosophers' virtue is "without a head" because they do not know God.

stances.summary: God sees everything, but our wills are free, so rewards and punishments are just. So resist vice, practise virtue, hope rightly and pray humbly.
stances.quote: Therefore, withstand vice, practise virtue, lift up your souls to right hopes, offer humble prayers to Heaven. Great is the necessity of righteousness laid upon you if ye will not hide it from yourselves, seeing that all your actions are done before the eyes of a Judge who seeth all things.
stances.translation: H. R. James, The Consolation of Philosophy, 1897 (Project Gutenberg)
stances.location: Book 5, prose 6 (the closing words of the book)
stances.context: Written in prison about 524 while awaiting execution. Lady Philosophy speaks, but the conclusion is the book's own. The sentences just before say "the freedom of man's will stands unshaken" and that "our hopes and prayers also are not fixed on God in vain", so prayer is part of the charge. The Consolation never mentions Christ or grace; Boethius's theological tractates are orthodox Catholic. Strength 1: this is a book about fate and free will, not a view on grace.

stances.summary: Free will is what made Adam the image of God. A person becomes the image of God by true knowledge and true conduct.
stances.quote: For if by Freewill Adam was the image of God, it is a most praiseworthy thing when, by true knowledge, and by true conduct, a man becomes the image of God.
stances.translation: C. W. Mitchell, S. Ephraim's Prose Refutations of Mani, Marcion and Bardaisan, vol. 1, 1912 (tertullian.org)
stances.context: Ephrem (died 373) is arguing against Mani and Bardaisan, whose systems made evil a matter of nature or fate; his stress on free will is aimed at them, not at grace. His hymns speak constantly of grace and gift, so this is one side of him. Strength 1.

stances.summary: The divine good is not far off. It is inside each of us, buried under cares and pleasures, and anyone who turns their mind to it finds it again.
stances.quote: the Divine good is not something apart from our nature, and is not removed far away from those who have the will to seek it; it is in fact within each of us, ignored indeed, and unnoticed while it is stifled beneath the cares and pleasures of life, but found again whenever we can turn our power of conscious thinking towards it.
stances.translation: William Moore and Henry Austin Wilson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 5, 1893 (CCEL)
stances.context: Written about 371. Gregory is reading the parable of the lost coin: the soul finds God's image by cleaning its own house. In the Great Catechism 31 (NPNF 2.5) he argues that God does not force anyone to believe, and that "it is not the goodness of God that is chargeable with the fact that the Faith is not engendered in all men, but rather the disposition of those by whom the preaching of the Word is received." Like the other Greek Fathers he held that God's help and human choice work together; his stress falls on freedom. Strength 1.

stances.original: Ἀγών ἐστι καὶ κόπος πολὺς τοῖς προσερχομένοις τῷ Θεῷ͵ τὰ πρῶτα· ἔπειτα δὲ͵ χαρὰ ἀνεκλάλητος. Ὥσπερ γὰρ οἱ πῦρ ἐξ άψαι βουλόμενοι͵ πρῶτον καπνίζονται καὶ δακρύουσι͵ καὶ οὕτως τοῦ ζητουμένου ἐπιτυγχάνουσι (καὶ γάρ φησιν͵ Ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν πῦρ καταναλίσκον ἐστίν)· οὕτως δεῖ καὶ ἡμᾶς εἰς ἑαυτοὺς τὸ θεῖον ἐξάψαι πῦρ μετὰ δακρύων καὶ πόνων
stances.summary: Coming to God is hard work at first and joy afterwards. Like lighting a fire, you must put up with the smoke and tears to get the flame.
stances.quote: At first there is struggle and much toil for those who come to God, and afterwards joy beyond words. For those who want to light a fire are first choked by the smoke and weep, and so they get what they are after (for it says, 'Our God is a consuming fire'). So we too must kindle the divine fire in ourselves with tears and toil.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Greek alphabetical collection of the Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Migne, PG 65), as transcribed on the page
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Apophthegmata Patrum), Greek alphabetical collection
stances.context: Syncletica lived in the 4th century near Alexandria. The fire she kindles is God Himself (Hebrews 12:29), so this is about perseverance in effort, not a theory that goodness is self-made. Strength 1. The English on the page is Benedicta Ward's copyrighted translation; the rendering here is from the Greek.

stances.summary: It depends on us and on God. We must choose the good first; God does not force the choice, but once we choose He helps us greatly, and His part is the greater.
stances.quote: It depends then on us, and on Him. For we must first choose the good; and then He leads us to His own. He does not anticipate our choice, lest our free-will should be outraged. But when we have chosen, then great is the assistance he brings to us.
stances.translation: Frederic Gardiner (ed.), NPNF 1st series vol. 14, 1889 (Oxford Library of the Fathers translation, revised)
stances.context: Preached at Constantinople about 403-404 and published after his death from shorthand notes. The same passage goes on: "it is ours to choose and to wish; but God's to complete and to bring to an end. Since therefore the greater part is of Him, he says all is of Him". In Homilies on Ephesians 4 (on Ephesians 2:8) he says that "the work of faith itself is not our own" (NPNF 1st series vol. 13, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230104.htm). So he is a clear middle voice: the first step is ours, the greater share God's. He wrote before the Pelagian quarrel. Note for display: this public-domain English has a lower-case "he" for God in the last sentence.

stances.summary: Grace and free will look like rivals but work together. Sometimes God starts the good in us, sometimes He sees a good wish in us and meets it; the main share still belongs to grace.
stances.quote: These two then; viz., the grace of God and free will seem opposed to each other, but really are in harmony, and we gather from the system of goodness that we ought to have both alike, lest if we withdraw one of them from man, we may seem to have broken the rule of the Church's faith
stances.translation: C. S. Gibson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11, 1894
stances.work: Conferences (Conference 13, of Abba Chaeremon, "On the Protection of God")
stances.context: Written at Marseille about 426-429, in the voice of the Egyptian Abba Chaeremon. Chapter 12 is headed "That a good will should not always be attributed to grace, nor always to man himself", and gives Zacchaeus and the good thief as people whose own desire came first, and Paul and Matthew as people grace seized first. Chapter 18 still says "the main share in our salvation is to be ascribed not to the merit of our own works but to heavenly grace". Prosper of Aquitaine attacked this conference, and the Council of Orange (529) later ruled that even the beginning of faith is God's gift. The label "Semi-Pelagian" for this view was coined more than a thousand years later. Cassian is honoured as a saint in the East and at Marseille.

stances.summary: Whether we live well is truly our choice, and God's commands are not pointless. But our perfection is not completed by us: God does far the greater part.
stances.quote: So also our own perfection is brought about, not as if we ourselves did nothing; for it is not completed by us, but God produces the greater part of it.
stances.translation: Frederick Crombie, ANF vol. 4, 1885 (translation of the Greek text preserved in the Philocalia)
stances.context: Written at Alexandria about 220-230. The whole chapter is a defence of free will against teachers who said souls are saved or lost by nature; in Rufinus's Latin version he says "it is our own doing whether we live rightly or not" (3.1.6). He then explains Romans 9:16 with a ship: sailors bring it to port, but winds and stars do far more, so "what is done by God is infinitely greater than what is done by ourselves". HETERODOX in part: some of Origen's other teachings were condemned in 553; on this point he is the pattern for the later Greek synergists.

stances.summary: A man working alone at freedom from passion gets nowhere. If he truly wants it and strives, God's power is added and he gets there. God works with willing souls.
stances.quote: For a man by himself working and toiling at freedom from passion achieves nothing. But if he plainly shows himself very desirous and earnest about this, he attains it by the addition of the power of God. For God conspires with willing souls.
stances.translation: William Wilson, ANF vol. 2, 1885
stances.work: Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?
stances.context: Written about 200, on Mark 10:27 ("with God all things are possible"). He goes on: "if they abandon their eagerness, the spirit which is bestowed by God is also restrained. For to save the unwilling is the part of one exercising compulsion; but to save the willing, that of one showing grace." ("Conspires" here means "breathes with, works together with".)

stances.summary: You did not make God; God makes you. Your part is to stay soft clay in His hands and not harden yourself, and the good He gives you, you must keep by your own striving.
stances.quote: Offer to Him your heart in a soft and tractable state, and preserve the form in which the Creator has fashioned you, having moisture in yourself, lest, by becoming hardened, you lose the impressions of His fingers.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut, ANF vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: Written about 180 against Gnostic teachers who said some people are good by nature. Just before: "For you did not make God, but God you." In 4.37 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0103437.htm) he insists on free will: the obedient "possess what is good, given indeed by God, but preserved by themselves", and the crown is precious because it is "acquired by our struggle". So he holds both: God is the maker, and we must keep what He gives.

stances.summary: Aim at what is perfect. When you truly want to do well, God is ready to help you.
stances.quote: As persons who are perfect, you should also aim at those things which are perfect. For when you are desirous to do well, God is also ready to assist you.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson, ANF vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: Written about 107-110 on the road to martyrdom in Rome. A passing line, so strength 1. In the same chapter he says he was counted worthy "not that I have any sense [of having deserved it], but by the grace of God".

stances.original: Bonum quippe quod agimus, et Dei est, et nostrum: Dei per praevenientem gratiam, nostrum per obsequentem liberam voluntatem. Si enim Dei non est, unde ei gratias in aeternum agimus? Rursum si nostrum non est, unde nobis retribui praemia speramus?
stances.summary: The good we do is both God's and ours. It is God's because His grace goes first, and ours because our free will follows. That is why we both thank Him and hope for a reward.
stances.quote: For the good which we do belongs both to God, and to ourselves. It is God’s by preventing grace, our own by the free will which follows. For if it is not of God, why do we return Him thanks for ever? Again, if it is not our own, why do we hope for rewards to be conferred on us?
stances.translation: Morals on the Book of Job, Library of the Fathers (Oxford: Parker, 1844-1850), as transcribed at lectionarycentral.com
stances.work: Moralia in Job (Morals on the Book of Job)
stances.context: Written about 579-595. "Preventing" is old English for "going before": grace comes first and the will follows. Just before, he says the elect's free will "is fashioned aright ... by the inspiration of grace", and the lost despised heaven "of their free will". So his middle view leans to grace first, unlike Chrysostom's. The Latin (Latin Wikisource, Moralia/VI) is given as the original.

stances.summary: God has already given us the power to keep every command, so nothing strange is asked of us and we have nothing to boast of. Using that power well is virtue; misusing it is vice.
stances.quote: as regards all the commandments given us by God, we have received already from Him power to keep them, that we may neither feel aggrieved as though anything strange were demanded of us, nor be elated as though we paid more than was given us.
stances.translation: W. K. Lowther Clarke, The Ascetic Works of Saint Basil (SPCK, 1925), archive.org scan
stances.context: Written in the 360s-370s for monks. Clarke's heading: "that the inclination and power to keep the Lord's commandments are in men naturally". The same answer says love of God is a seed planted at creation which his pupils, "by God's grace", nourish and bring to perfection, and it continues: "by this power, if we work rightly and fittingly, we fulfil in godly manner the life of virtue". The power is God's gift; its use is ours. Basil's Homily on Humility, often quoted for the grace side, was not checked here (see notes).

stances.original: Δαβὶδ ὅτε μετὰ τοῦ λέοντος συνέβαλε͵ τοῦ λαρυγγίου αὐτοῦ κατέσχεν αὐτὸν͵ καὶ εὐθέως ἀπέκτεινεν αὐτόν. Ἐὰν οὖν καὶ ἡμεῖς κατά σχωμεν τοῦ λαρυγγίου καὶ τῆς κοιλίας ἑαυτῶν͵ νι κῶμεν διὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ τὸν ἀόρατον λέοντα.
stances.summary: Take yourself firmly in hand, as David gripped the lion by the throat; but the victory over the unseen enemy comes through God.
stances.quote: When David fought with the lion, he seized it by the throat and killed it at once. So if we too take hold of our own throat and belly, we conquer the invisible lion through God.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Greek alphabetical collection of the Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Migne, PG 65), as transcribed on the page
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Apophthegmata Patrum), Greek alphabetical collection
stances.context: Poemen (5th century, Scetis) is the most quoted abba in the collection. "Throat and belly" means speech and appetite. Another saying (Poemen 36) lists the soul's tools as throwing yourself before God, not measuring your own progress, and leaving self-will behind. The English on the page is Benedicta Ward's copyrighted translation; the rendering here is from the Greek.

stances.summary: A bad tree only bears good fruit if something better is grafted in. That graft is God's grace, stronger than nature, working through our free will.
stances.quote: This will be the power of the grace of God, more potent indeed than nature, exercising its sway over the faculty that underlies itself within us — even the freedom of our will
stances.translation: Peter Holmes, ANF vol. 3, 1885
stances.work: A Treatise on the Soul (De anima)
stances.context: Written about 210-213, in his Montanist period (HETERODOX in that period). Just before: "A corrupt tree will never yield good fruit, unless the better nature be grafted into it". Elsewhere (On Exhortation to Chastity 2, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0405.htm, also Montanist) he warns against blaming God for everything "as to make us fail to understand that there is a something in our own power", and says the will to sin "has its source in ourselves". So: sin is ours, the change of nature is grace working on a free will.

stances.original: Quod ergo credimus, nostrum est, quod autem bonum operamur, illius qui credentibus in se dat Spiritum Sanctum
stances.summary: EARLY VIEW, later withdrawn: believing is our own act; the good works that follow are God's, who gives the Spirit to believers.
stances.quote: So the fact that we believe is our own; but the good we do is His who gives the Holy Spirit to those who believe in Him.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Latin (Migne text on Latin Wikisource)
stances.work: Exposition of Certain Propositions from the Epistle to the Romans
stances.location: the proposition on Romans 9:11-13 (numbered 60 in modern editions)
stances.context: Written in 394-395 while Augustine was a priest. He reversed it in To Simplician (396). In On the Predestination of the Saints 3.7 (428-429) he quotes this very sentence and calls it his error: "I myself also was convinced when I was in a similar error, thinking that faith whereby we believe in God is not God's gift, but that it is in us from ourselves" (NPNF 1st series vol. 5, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/15121.htm). He says the same in his Retractations 1.23. This is the clearest documented change of mind on this question among the Fathers. The English version of this early work (Landes, 1982) is copyrighted.

stances.summary: We cannot even do what God commands unless He gives it. So he prays: give what You command, and then command what You will. God does not make us good without our will, but it is God who makes the will good.
stances.quote: And my whole hope is only in Your exceeding great mercy. Give what You command, and command what You will.
stances.translation: J. G. Pilkington, NPNF 1st series vol. 1, 1887 (as revised for New Advent)
stances.context: Written about 397-400, in a prayer about self-control. The line is repeated in 10.31.45 and 10.37.60. Pelagius heard it quoted at Rome, "could not bear" it and nearly quarrelled with the bishop who quoted it (Augustine, Gift of Perseverance 20.53, NPNF, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/15122.htm). His settled teaching, from 396 on: "He operates, therefore, without us, in order that we may will; but when we will, and so will that we may act, He co-operates with us. We can, however, ourselves do nothing to effect good works of piety without Him" (On Grace and Free Will 17.33, 426-427, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1510.htm). He never denied free will: in Sermon 169.11.13, preached against the Pelagians, he says "He who made you without you does not justify you without you. He made you without your knowing; He justifies you with your willing. Yet it is He who justifies, so that the righteousness is not your own", and "If God made you a man, and you make yourself righteous, you are making something better than God made" (own rendering of "Si hominem te fecit Deus, et justum tu te facis; melius aliquid facis quam fecit Deus. Sed sine te fecit te Deus. Non enim adhibuisti aliquem consensum, ut te faceret Deus. Quomodo consentiebas qui non eras? Qui ergo fecit te sine te, non te justificat sine te. Ergo fecit nescientem, justificat volentem. Tamen ipse justificat, ne sit justitia tua", Latin Wikisource, Sermones de Scripturis (ed. Migne)/2). See his separate EARLY stance for the view he gave up.

stances.original: Dei est, inquam, Dei omne, quod possumus. inde uiuimus, inde pollemus
stances.summary: Before baptism he thought he could never break his habits. Afterwards what had seemed impossible became possible, and he credits none of it to himself: all our power is from God.
stances.quote: so that now we sin not is the beginning of the work of faith, whereas that we sinned before was the result of human error. All our power is of God; I say, of God.
stances.translation: Robert Ernest Wallis, ANF vol. 5, 1886
stances.context: Written about 246, soon after his baptism, describing his own conversion: he had indulged his sins "as if they were actually parts of me", despairing of change, until "what had been thought impossible" became "capable of being achieved". The same sentence says we can only be grateful "for whatever we do not ascribe to man's virtue but declare to be the gift of God". His Testimonies 3.4 has the heading "That we must boast in nothing, since nothing is our own" (ANF 5, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/050712c.htm), which became Augustine's favourite witness against Pelagius. The Latin original is Hartel's text on Latin Wikisource ("Ad Donatum").

stances.original: Non enim in potestate nostra cor nostrum et cogitationes nostrae, quae improviso offusae mentem animumque confundunt, atque alio trahunt quam tu proposueris
stances.summary: We talk easily about leaving the world behind, but our own hearts and thoughts are not in our control. They pull us away against our purpose, so this cannot be done without God's help.
stances.quote: For our heart and our thoughts are not in our own power, and these, poured forth unexpectedly, confuse our mind and soul, and draw them in a different direction from that which you have proposed to yourself
stances.translation: Peter Holmes and Robert Ernest Wallis, revised by Benjamin B. Warfield, NPNF 1st series vol. 5, 1887 (Ambrose as quoted by Augustine)
stances.work: On Flight from the World (De fuga saeculi), as quoted verbatim by Augustine in On the Gift of Perseverance
stances.location: On Flight from the World 1.1; Gift of Perseverance 8.20 (chapter 20 on New Advent)
stances.context: Ambrose wrote the treatise in the late 380s or early 390s; Augustine, his convert, quotes it in 428-429 and says Ambrose taught that the world must be fled "not by the body, but by the heart ... which he argued could not be done except by God's help". Augustine also quotes Ambrose on Luke 1:3: "For not alone by human will did it seem good, but as it pleased Him who speaks in me, Christ, who effects that that which is good may also seem good to us" (Gift of Perseverance 19.49). Ambrose also preached hard effort; the line is about thoughts and desires, so strength 1. The Latin is from Augustine's text (De dono perseverantiae, Latin Wikisource).

stances.original: Velle et currere meum est: sed ipsum meum, sine Dei semper auxilio non erit meum.
stances.summary: He gladly keeps free will, but says he is powerless unless God keeps giving His help. Willing and running are his, yet they stop being his without God's constant aid.
stances.quote: To will and to run are mine, but they will cease to be mine unless God brings me His continual aid.
stances.translation: W. H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W. G. Martley, NPNF 2nd series vol. 6, 1893
stances.context: Written in 414 against Pelagius, followed in 415 by his Dialogue against the Pelagians in three books, in which his spokesman Atticus says: "we who preserve free will for man, but so limit it that we do not deny the assistance of God in each action" (Dialogue 1.5, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/30111.htm). In the same letter: "we are powerless unless He continually preserves in us His own gift", and "It is not enough for me that he has given me grace once; He must give it me always." His formula keeps willing and running as ours, so he is close to Chrysostom on the mechanism, but his whole purpose here is to deny that goodness is our own achievement. The Latin original is from Latin Wikisource, Epistolae (Hieronymus)/4, Letter 133 (https://la.wikisource.org/wiki/Epistolae_(Hieronymus)/4).

stances.summary: Against people who credit all their success to themselves: even wanting the good needs God's help, and choosing the right is itself His gift. We are our own masters, but our salvation is from God.
stances.quote: such are taught by this word that even to wish well needs help from God; or rather that even to choose what is right is divine and a gift of the mercy of God. For it is necessary both that we should be our own masters and also that our salvation should be of God.
stances.translation: Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow, NPNF 2nd series vol. 7, 1894
stances.context: Preached at Constantinople in 380. He is explaining "to whom it is given" and Romans 9:16, aimed at "some who are so proud of their successes that they attribute all to themselves". He keeps free choice ("it is given to those who are called and to those who incline that way") but ends: "However much you may run, however much you may wrestle, yet you need one to give the crown." A middle view leaning clearly to grace, so strength 1.

stances.original: Bonum aliquid in se cum viderit, Deo adplicet, non sibi. Malum vero semper a se factum sciat et sibi reputet.
stances.summary: If you see any good in yourself, credit it to God. The evil you do, own as yours. Where nature falls short, ask God for His grace.
stances.quote: If he sees some good in himself, let him credit it to God, not to himself. But let him know that evil is always his own doing, and count it as his own.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Latin (The Latin Library text of the Rule)
stances.location: chapter 4 (the tools of good works), verses 42-43
stances.context: Written about 530-540. The Prologue says the same twice (own renderings): those who fear the Lord "are not puffed up by their good observance, but judge that the good in them cannot come from themselves but is done by the Lord", and "what our nature finds less possible, let us ask the Lord to bid the help of His grace serve us" (Latin: "et quod minus habet in nos natura possibile, rogemus Dominum, ut gratiæ suæ iubeat nobis adiutorium ministrare."). Yet the Rule is a school of hard effort: "we must run and act now what will profit us for ever". The chapter 4 line is adapted from the earlier Rule of the Master. Pre-1929 English translations exist (Gasquet 1909, Hunter Blair 1886) but were not loaded, so the rendering is from the Latin.

stances.summary: Antony's victory over temptation was really Christ's work in him, so every true fighter can say with Paul: not I, but the grace of God with me.
stances.quote: This was Antony's first struggle against the devil, or rather this victory was the Saviour's work in Antony
stances.translation: H. Ellershaw, NPNF 2nd series vol. 4, 1892
stances.location: chapter 7 (Athanasius writing in his own voice)
stances.context: Written about 357-362. In chapter 5 Athanasius says "the Lord was working with Antony", so that all who truly fight can say "not I but the grace of God which was with me" (1 Corinthians 15:10). He also records, without correcting it, Antony's teaching that virtue needs only our willingness (chapter 20). So Athanasius held effort and grace together, and in his own voice gives the credit to Christ. Strength 1.

stances.original: Ὁ Θεὸς͵ μὴ ἐγκαταλίπῃς με· οὐδὲν ἐποίησα ἐνώπιόν σου ἀγαθόν· ἀλλὰ δός μοι κατὰ τὴν χρηστότητά σου βα λεῖν ἀρχήν
stances.summary: Even after years in the desert he prays that he has done nothing good yet, and asks God for the grace to make a beginning.
stances.quote: O God, do not forsake me. I have done nothing good in Your sight. But grant me, in Your kindness, to make a beginning.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Greek alphabetical collection of the Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Migne, PG 65), as transcribed on the page
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Apophthegmata Patrum), Greek alphabetical collection
stances.context: Arsenius (died about 449) had been tutor in the imperial palace before becoming a monk at Scetis. His servants overheard this prayer while demons were troubling him. It is a prayer, not a doctrine, so strength 1. Benedicta Ward's copyrighted English adds "of good"; the Greek says only "to lay a beginning".

stances.original: Ὁ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ σάρκα βουληθεὶς πολεμῆσαι, ἢ νικῆσαι ἐξ ἑαυτοῦ, εἰς μάτην τρέχει. Ἐὰν γὰρ μὴ Κύριος καταλύσῃ οἶκον σαρκὸς, καὶ οἰκοδομήσῃ οἶκον ψυχῆς, εἰς μάτην ἠγρύπνησε, καὶ ἐνήστευσεν ὁ καταλύων. Ἀνάθου Κυρίῳ τὴν τῆς φύσεως ἀσθένειαν, ἐπιγνοὺς εἰς ἅπαν τὴν οἰκείαν ἀδυναμίαν, καὶ λήψῃ χάρισμα σωφροσύνης ἀνεπαισθήτως
stances.summary: Whoever tries to master his body by his own strength runs in vain. Hand your weakness to the Lord, admit you cannot do it, and He will give the gift.
stances.quote: Whoever wants to fight his own flesh, or to conquer it by himself, runs in vain. For unless the Lord pulls down the house of the flesh and builds the house of the soul, the one pulling it down has kept vigil and fasted in vain. Offer the weakness of your nature to the Lord, fully admitting your powerlessness, and you will receive the gift of chastity without noticing.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Greek (Migne, PG 88, as transcribed on Greek Wikisource)
stances.context: Written at Sinai in the first half of the 7th century. The line echoes Psalm 127:1 and is about chastity, the struggle where monks felt their weakness most; the Ladder as a whole is a demanding programme of effort in thirty steps. No English translation before 1929 was found; the English in use (Moore 1959, Luibheid and Russell 1982) is copyrighted.

stances.original: Μακάριος άνθρωπος ο γινώσκων την εαυτού ασθένειαν. Διότι αύτη η γνώσις γίνεται αυτώ θεμέλιος και ρίζα καϊ αρχή πάσης αγαθωσύνης.
stances.summary: Blessed is the one who knows his weakness: that knowledge is the root of all good. Knowing we need God's help drives us to pray, prayer makes us humble, and then His help comes near.
stances.quote: For the help of God is necessary for deliverance. When he knows that he needs divine help, he will frequently pray. And by much beseeching the heart becomes humble.
stances.translation: A. J. Wensinck, Mystic Treatises by Isaac of Nineveh (Amsterdam, 1923), archive.org scan
stances.location: Treatise 7 in Wensinck (Homily 21 in the Greek collection)
stances.context: Isaac (7th century) was briefly bishop of Nineveh in the Church of the East, then a hermit. The treatise opens: "Blessed is the man who knows his weakness. This knowledge becomes for him the foundation and the beginning [of his coming] unto all good and beautiful things." Later it adds a two-way note: "as he brings near his spirit unto God, He comes nigh unto him with His gifts." The original given is the opening sentence in the Greek version (Greek Wikisource, Ασκητικά/Λόγος ΚΑ, https://el.wikisource.org/wiki/%CE%91%CF%83%CE%BA%CE%B7%CF%84%CE%B9%CE%BA%CE%AC/%CE%9B%CF%8C%CE%B3%CE%BF%CF%82%20%CE%9A%CE%91); Isaac wrote in Syriac. Strength 1: the stress is on humility and prayer rather than a theory of grace.

stances.original: Ὁ λῃστὴς ἐν τῷ σταυρῷ ἦν͵ καὶ ἀπὸ λόγου ἑνὸς ἐδικαιώθη· καὶ Ἰούδας μετὰ τῶν ἀποστόλων συνηριθμημένος ἦν͵ καὶ ἐν νυκτὶ μιᾷ ἀπώλεσε πάντα τὸν κάματον͵ καὶ κατέβη ἐξ οὐρανῶν εἰς ᾅδην. Διὸ μηδεὶς εὐπραγῶν καυχάσθω· πάντες γὰρ οἱ πεποιθότες ἐφ΄ ἑαυτοῖς ἔπεσον
stances.person: Xanthias, desert father of Scetis (not in the results pool)
stances.summary: The thief was saved by one word and Judas lost everything in one night. So no one doing well should boast, because all who trusted in themselves fell.
stances.quote: The thief was on the cross and was justified by a single word. Judas was numbered with the apostles, yet in a single night he lost all his labour and went down from heaven to Hades. So let no one who is doing well boast. For all who trusted in themselves have fallen.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Greek alphabetical collection of the Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Migne, PG 65), as transcribed on the page
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Apophthegmata Patrum), Greek alphabetical collection
stances.context: A 4th-5th century monk of Scetis, known only from the Sayings. Recorded because it states the warning plainly; not a candidate result.

splits_fathers: Real voices on all three sides, and a genuine historical fight. AGREE: Pelagius and Caelestius argued it outright and were condemned (416-431); Antony's speech in the Life of Antony ("virtue has need at our hands of willingness alone") and Lactantius ("virtue is altogether our own") say it bluntly in passing; Justin, Ephrem, Gregory of Nyssa and Boethius stress free will, but against fate or determinism rather than against grace. MIXED, the largest group and the Greek norm: Clement, Irenaeus, Ignatius, Origen, Basil, Chrysostom, Cassian, Poemen and Gregory the Great say God and the person work together; Chrysostom and Cassian put the first move with us, Gregory the Great puts it with grace, and nearly all say God's share is the greater. DISAGREE: Augustine (after 396), Cyprian, Ambrose, Jerome, Gregory of Nazianzus, Benedict, Climacus, Isaac, Arsenius and Athanasius say the good in us is God's gift and warn against trusting our own work. After the Council of Orange (529) the Latin West ruled against even Cassian's middle view; the Greek East never had a Pelagian controversy and kept the language of cooperation (synergy). Almost no one on any side denies free will, and almost no one on any side says effort is unnecessary; the real question is whose share is larger and who moves first.
splits_people_today: Well split, which makes it a useful item. Many ordinary people, religious or not, would agree: self-help culture treats character as habits you build by choice and effort, and many churchgoers answer surveys in the same direction. Committed Reformed and Lutheran Protestants would disagree strongly ("grace alone"). Catholics and Orthodox Christians would often pick a middle answer (grace first, then cooperation), so they may hesitate on "mainly". A second group would disagree for secular reasons: people who think character is mostly shaped by genes, upbringing and circumstance. So disagreement comes from two very different directions (grace and determinism), and the quiz writer should know that a "disagree" does not by itself mean a grace-first Christian.

misattributions.line: Pray as though everything depended on God. Work as though everything depended on you.
misattributions.truth: Not found in Augustine's works. The saying descends from a maxim attributed to Ignatius of Loyola in Gabriel Hevenesi's Scintillae Ignatianae (1705), whose Latin wording puts it the other way round (trust God as if all depended on you, work as if all depended on God). From background knowledge; not re-checked against a source in this session.

misattributions.line: Without God, we cannot; without us, God will not.
misattributions.truth: A loose modern paraphrase. The real line is Sermon 169.11.13: "Qui ergo fecit te sine te, non te justificat sine te" ("He who made you without you does not justify you without you"), which goes on "Yet it is He who justifies, so that the righteousness is not your own". The paraphrase drops that second half. Verified in the Latin (Latin Wikisource, Sermones de Scripturis (ed. Migne)/2).

misattributions.line: Ought implies can / If I ought, I can.
misattributions.truth: The slogan is Kant's. The nearest early wording is in the Definitions ascribed to Caelestius and quoted by Augustine: "If he ought, he is able; if he is not able, then he ought not" (On Man's Perfection in Righteousness 3.5). Augustine himself was unsure whether they were Caelestius's own. Pelagius makes the same point in other words (Letter to Demetrias 16).

misattributions.line: Letter to Demetrias (the letter on the power of human nature)
misattributions.truth: It is by Pelagius, who claimed it in a letter to Pope Innocent quoted by Augustine (On the Grace of Christ 1.40). It survived by being copied under Jerome's name and is printed among Jerome's spurious letters in Migne, PL 30. A different, anti-Pelagian "Letter to Demetrias on true humility" (PL 55, ascribed to Leo I or Prosper) is sometimes confused with it.

misattributions.line: God helps those who help themselves.
misattributions.truth: Not in Scripture or in any Father found here. It is an old proverb (compare Aesop and Sophocles) made famous in English by Algernon Sidney (1698) and Benjamin Franklin's Poor Richard's Almanack (1736). From background knowledge; not re-checked in this session.

notes: For the quiz: this is one of the best-split topics among the Fathers, with Pelagius versus Augustine as the famous pair (Pelagius nearly quarrelled over "Give what You command"). Good nearest/farthest reveals: Pelagius or Antony (agree), Chrysostom or Cassian (middle), Augustine, Cyprian or Climacus (disagree). Keep the statement generic in the quiz; "mainly" is the word that separates the middle group from Pelagius, so a softer or harder wording will move Chrysostom, Cassian and Origen. Fairness: say that Pelagius did speak of grace (he meant nature, law, teaching and forgiveness) and that Augustine did affirm free will; neither side was a caricature. Several agree voices (Justin, Ephrem, Gregory of Nyssa, Boethius) were arguing against fate, not against grace, so weight them low. Display: two public-domain quotes have a lower-case "he" for God (Chrysostom's "the assistance he brings"; Jerome's "he has given me grace once" in the context field); the site's capital rule should be applied when shown. Not checked, as leads only: Basil's Homily on Humility (often quoted for "justified by faith in Christ alone"), Pelagius's Commentary on Romans, Prosper of Aquitaine's reply to Cassian, Julian of Eclanum, Hilary on Psalm 118, Macarian homilies. Nothing relevant was found for Perpetua, Hippolytus, Novatian, Martin of Tours, Paulinus of Nola, Macrina, Moses the Black or Evagrius on this question. Encoding: the lectionarycentral page is windows-1252 (the apostrophe in "God’s" is byte 0x92); the ldysinger pages declare windows-1252 but carry the Greek as UTF-8, and their Greek has stray spaces inside some words (for example "βα λεῖν"), which are copied as they appear.
